Analyses in support of such facility freeze confirmation activities may involve confirmation that equipment has not physically moved (e.g. by comparing SLAM maps), but may also involve assessing radiological signatures, which may be expected to evolve due to the radioactivity of the material in question. Full-spectral SDF algorithms that provide quantitative estimates of Plutonium-containing spectra and their shielding characteristics would be helpful. Free-moving tritium mapping would be a great technology, but is technologically very difficult (if not impossible). From the perspective of SDF R&D needs, the UVT is quite similar to PVT in that source localization and characterization are paramount, hold-up identification and characterization is important, adding quantitative capabilities is desirable, and tools that could support facility freeze confirmation are of value. A major difference between the UVT and PVT’s needs is that UVT typically works with lower radioactivity material, expects significantly less neutron activity, and has interest in automated uranium enrichment, chemical processing, and age determination (rather than Pu-containing material). The TSVT would likely operate in excavated tunnels and may benefit from thorough characterization of radioactive profiles of subsidence craters. SDF-base SLAM capabilities may benefit TSVT as could attenuation-aware mapping, where very high-activity sources may be locatable even through meters of rock. Test sites are often large and may present unsafe terrain, which would both benefit from ground and aerial robot-based technologies. Overall, the TSVT’s use cases are least well understood by the authors of this report due to the team’s relative newness and limited development of technological needs. 4.6 Nuclear Facility Operations Operating nuclear facilities have a variety of activities that could benefit from free-moving radiological data fusion: • Hold up • Criticality safety • Waste characterization • Dose rate monitoring, potentially in high-rate environments • Material security Many of these uses overlap with CONOPs described in the assessment of other applications’ SDF R&D needs above, but waste characterization and criticality safety are more specific to facility operations and will be elaborated upon here. Waste characterization precedes any shipment of waste from a nuclear facility to a storage/deposition facility and is important to ensure public safety during transport and that the receiving facility is able to safely handle the received materials. Because most mixed radioactive waste is highly nonhomogeneous, activity determinations are typically made using intentionally LBNL Report #2001653 conservative assumptions. For example, the emission rate observed from a container is assumed to be due to a point-like source in the middle of the container and therefore subject to the maximal attenuation based on average areal density of the container contents as determined from the known container mass.
